It creates the competitive pressure between localized theories that eventually forces the emergence of a higher-level synthesis.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the system has no mechanism for dialectical resolution or cross-lineage communication, the clash remains unresolved, and the cross-cutting explanation is never discovered.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the boundary problems are never allocated to both lineages simultaneously or sequentially, the clash never occurs.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If one lineage can eventually solve all problems recursively using its own primitives, the competitive pressure dissipates, and no higher-level synthesis is required.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Cross-cutting explanations are not found by searching a homogeneous space of primitives. They are synthesized when two incompatible, highly optimized local theories (developed in isolation via ownership) clash on a boundary problem. The allocation policy ensures these local theories become sufficiently rigid and distinct. The cross-cutting explanation is then the dialectical resolution of this clash. Without ownership-based allocation, the system would converge prematurely to a shallow consensus, suppressing the discovery of deep cross-cutting explanations.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
